extracted.intended_audience: concert pianists, piano teachers, and serious piano students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and standards for piano practice, technique, interpretation, memorization, repertoire maintenance, and pedagogy as given by concert pianists and teachers. Covers teacher responsibilities, daily technical routines, relaxation/posture, learning and polishing pieces, and classroom/teaching organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher's corrective and constructive role
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher's work is both corrective and constructive: he must see what is wrong and be able to correct it, find the weak and deficient parts and build them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher should diagnose weak spots like a physician and have remedies that fit the needs of each pupil; adapt teaching to individual pupil's defects rather than applying one-size-fits-all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized remedies for each pupil
rubrics_metrics.description: Have some remedy at his command that will fit the needs of each pupil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each pupil differently because hands, intelligence, and character vary; individualized treatment is an advantage to the teacher and necessary for progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use etudes sparingly ('homeopathic doses')
rubrics_metrics.description: I give very few etudes, and those I administer in homeopathic doses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to play through a mass of etudes to become a good pianist; much technic may be learned from the pieces themselves, though scales and arpeggios must form part of the daily routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily scales and arpeggios
rubrics_metrics.description: Scales and arpeggios must form part of the daily routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scales and arpeggios each day even if etude usage is limited; use these as core technical maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain repertoire by teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The pianist who does much teaching is in a sense taught by his pupils; in teaching their repertoire I keep up my own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching students' pieces exposes the teacher to recurring technical and interpretive problems and helps devise methods to overcome them; beware that repeated exposure may make pieces seem less fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental rehearsal of programs
rubrics_metrics.description: I go over my pieces mentally, especially if I am playing an entirely new program which I have never played before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mental practice to prepare for new programs; less necessary for familiar repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improvising to cover forgotten passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvising on a well-known work is rather a dangerous thing to do in order to improve a bad case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a passage is forgotten in performance, ad-libbing risks inconsistency and confusion; practice 'bridges' only when you can reliably remember what you will play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve vital energy in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most necessary things is the conserving of vital energy in piano practise; the wrong way is to continually practise the piece as though you were playing it in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice at medium tone and without full pedaling most of the time so you can sustain long daily practice (5–6 hours) without fatigue; reserve full force for occasional complete run-throughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to practise long hours without fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: I think a pianist should be able to practise five or six hours daily without fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Husband vital force in routine practice to allow demanding public programs to be played without weariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice effects intermittently, not always full force
rubrics_metrics.description: Every effect you wish to make must be thoroughly studied, must be in mind, and used at intervals whenever a complete performance of the piece is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study expressive effects deliberately and incorporate them periodically into practice rather than executing everything at full intensity each repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control impulse to 'let loose' in rehearsals
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often difficult to control the impulse to 'let loose' if the work is an exciting one; one may intend to run through quietly but find oneself playing with full force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate restraint in rehearsals; practice the intended reduced dynamic plan so you don't unintentionally exhaust yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept diversity of touch methods, emphasize arm weight
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to be a diversity of opinion resulting from various ways of touching the keys—some players using the tip and others the ball of the finger... Of course players generally, and teachers also, agree on the employment of arm weight in playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple valid hand/touch approaches (tip vs. ball vs. flat hand) while maintaining arm-weight principles as central to technique; adapt to what is natural and effective for the player.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring out the composer's meaning plus personal inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The vital thing in piano playing is to bring out the composer's meaning, plus your own inspiration and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study deeply into the composer's idea and also inject your own intensity so the performance moves listeners; balance fidelity and individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coldly calculated, mechanical dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: A master who apportions so many grains of power for forte, mezzo, piano... puts a damper on individuality and enthusiasm; such playing does not really warm the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce interpretation to formulaic dynamic prescriptions—favor expressive judgment and individuality over mechanical application of dynamic labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach tonal contrasts and tone color early
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe in teaching tonal contrasts and tone color even to a beginner; the child should form a concept of forte and piano and get away from monotony of mezzo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce concepts of loud/soft and tone color from the start, using small descriptive pieces to illustrate contrasts (e.g., loud closing phrase followed by soft echo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve enthusiasm for modern music and diversify repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: I thoroughly believe in preserving one's enthusiasm for modern music... studying new works keeps me young and buoyant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include contemporary works alongside classical repertoire to maintain freshness and broaden interpretive perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form an ideal conception and 'live' with a new piece
rubrics_metrics.description: In learning a new work I first study it very slowly, trying to become familiar with its meaning. I form my concept of it and live with it for months before I care to bring it forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work slowly, build an ideal interpretation in detail, and test it repeatedly in public settings until the interpretation crystallizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the audience as a testing and refining teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience is the greatest teacher an artist can have; I have learned more from this teacher than from any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public performance feedback to learn what moves listeners, refine climaxes and colorings, and stabilize interpretation through repeated trials; avoid changing the interpretation at each repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'music-knowers' when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Music-knowers are preferable because even if very critical, they recognize and appreciate the points you make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek audiences with informed listeners when you want detailed response and recognition of interpretive subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain natural hand position and individual technique
rubrics_metrics.description: I have always taken positions of body, arms, hands and fingers which seemed to me most natural and easy... The question should be: What has the player in himself, what can he accomplish?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect each player's natural ergonomic choices while guiding them to sound technical principles; avoid slavish imitation of teacher lineage as the primary criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular technical practice using canonical etudes and repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: I give an hour or more a day to technical practise. I use Chopin's Etudes constantly... Liszt Etudes Transcendantes, and, of course, Bach. I keep all these etudes in daily practise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a core set of technical studies active in daily work to ensure readiness for recitals; add special pieces as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow study initially for new works
rubrics_metrics.description: In learning a new work I first study it very slowly, trying to become familiar with its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin at slow tempos to internalize structure and meaning before increasing speed; develop concept prior to polished runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation as the keynote of modern playing
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxation is a hobby with me; I believe in absolute freedom in every part of the arm anatomy, from the shoulder down to the finger-tips. Stiffness is the most reprehensible thing in piano playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and practice complete relaxation of shoulders, arm, wrist and fingers; check for tension frequently and correct posture and motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach relaxation and wrist motion from the start
rubrics_metrics.description: I use the principle of relaxation first of all, loosening arms and wrists. This principle can be taught to the youngest pupil. The wrist is elevated and lowered, as the hand is formed on the keys in its five-finger position, with arched knuckles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce simple relaxation and wrist mobility exercises early; form arched knuckles and a loose wrist as foundational habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor fingers close to keys and weight-based power
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not believe in the so-called finger stroke; on the contrary I advocate fingers close to the keys, clinging to them whenever you can... get all the power needed by grasping the keys with weight and pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize weight and pressure rather than exaggerated finger lift or percussive 'stroke'; avoid unnecessary preparatory lifts in chord playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorize phrase-by-phrase at the instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: I do it phrase by phrase, and at the instrument... If the piece is very difficult I take a short passage of two or three measures and play each hand separately and then together; then repeat from memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small-unit memorization, practicing hands separately as needed, repeat with and without score until phrase memory is secure; if away from piano, think through from the notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require broad general education and musical-literary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The student should have a good all-round education... the music pupil also needs to know musical literature, history and biography, to be familiar with the lives and writings of the great composers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage study of theory, history, biographies and writings (e.g., Schumann's letters) to deepen musical understanding and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate technical work initially (devote early weeks to technic)
rubrics_metrics.description: I require that nothing but technical exercises be used for the first nine, ten, or twelve weeks... begin with simplest exercises, one finger at a time, then scales, arpeggios, chords and octaves until principles mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pupils lacking foundational technique, focus intensively on technical exercises for a set period to build strength and correct positions before moving to repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Czerny (and similar) studies for fundamental application
rubrics_metrics.description: For application of all principles, the studies of Czerny, Op. 299, 740, and others, offer unequaled opportunity. They are simple, direct, and give the student a chance for undivided attention to every position taken and to every motion made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ Czerny and similar foundational studies to isolate technical motions and instill consistent positions and motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monthly classes and memory performance for concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a month my assistant teachers bring their pupils to play for me, and we have a class in piano teaching... On the first Saturday I have my own pupils here for a class; everything is played from memory, not a printed note is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize regular group classes and memory recitals to develop concentration, stage practice, and to expose pupils to peer learning; expect initial difficulty which improves with repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posture and arm mechanism: arched knuckles, loose wrists, arm swing
rubrics_metrics.description: Hands were well arched at the knuckles, fingers curved—with adequate action at the knuckle joint; wrists in normal position, and extremely loose; the whole arm swung from the shoulder and poised over the keys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for arched knuckles, curved fingers, loose yet responsive wrists, and arm movement initiated from the shoulder so the arm can adjust to composition requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign appropriate weight to every note
rubrics_metrics.description: Every note had its amount of hand or arm weight. The tone quality was full and singing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to consider the necessary hand/arm weight for each note to achieve a singing tone and appropriate emphasis; avoid uniform, mechanical touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build up the hand and equalize weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: I aim to build up the hand, to make it strong and dependable in every part, to fill out the weak places and equalize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify individual weak fingers/areas and use focused exercises to strengthen and equalize them for dependable technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive teacher method: accretion of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The progressive teacher's method must be one of accretion. He gains ideas from many methods and sources, and these he assimilates and makes practical for his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should study many approaches, assimilate useful ideas, and originate adaptations suited to their pupils rather than rigidly following a single dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and remedy stiff wrists and arms early
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the pupils were afflicted with stiff wrists and arms, and this stiffness must be remedied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen for stiffness in students and apply relaxation/weight/position exercises to correct rigidity as a priority in early instruction.
